rules.title: Challenge the model behind the request
rules.what: When a request names an AI approach, check whether the task needs a model at all, whether this is the smallest one that clears the quality bar, and whether the approach fits or was just first to mind.
rules.why: Deterministic code answers the same question for near-zero marginal cost, every time. Routing a deterministic task to a model pays compute, latency and energy for a slower, less reliable version of the same answer.
rules.how: Before building: name the ambiguity the model resolves. No ambiguity, no model (or a much smaller one). Raise the argument once, take the answer, deliver what the user decides.

verify.how: The AI decision records: the ambiguity, the smaller alternative tested, and why it did or did not clear the quality bar.

limits: A user who has heard the argument and still wants the model is making a decision, not a mistake.

rules.title: Size the model to the task
rules.what: Pick the smallest model that meets the quality bar for the task; route simple tasks to lighter models and reserve large ones for what measurably needs them.
rules.why: Inference cost scales with model size across every request; using a large model for a task a small one does well pays the difference forever, and quality does not care about the extra parameters.
rules.how: Evaluate candidate models on the task's acceptance set, choose the smallest passing one, document the evaluation, re-test when models change.

verify.how: Evaluation records: task set, candidate models, scores, cost per task; chosen model is the smallest passing.

limits: Quality bars are project decisions; the rule forces the evidence, not the choice.

rules.title: Trim the input before trimming anything else
rules.what: Send the model only the context the task needs: minimal prompts, retrieved-not-dumped documents, no whole files where excerpts suffice.
rules.why: Prompt processing costs with every token, on every request, for every user. Most prompts pay for context the model does not use.
rules.how: State the goal and a path to the details instead of pasting everything; retrieve on demand; filter and trim documents before embedding; cap and reuse system prompts.

verify.how: Input token count per task measured and within the stated budget for the quality level.

limits: Insufficient context costs accuracy; trim to the measured minimum, not to zero.

rules.title: Cache AI results where stable
rules.what: Cache the results of AI calls that repeat with the same inputs: embeddings for repeated documents, answers to repeated questions, classification of unchanged items.
rules.why: Identical inputs produce identical outputs at full cost; caching them is the cheapest inference saving there is.
rules.how: Content-addressed cache keys (hash of prompt + model + version), TTL on volatile contexts, bounded store (NR-ARCH-006).

verify.how: Cache hit rate on production traffic; duplicated inference count trending to the intended floor.

limits: Personalised or time-sensitive outputs must not be served stale; mark cacheability explicitly.

rules.title: Batch requests
rules.what: Batch independent inference requests (batch APIs, grouped embeddings, vectorised inputs) instead of one-by-one calls; batch only items with compatible latency budgets.
rules.why: Batched inference fills the accelerator's parallel capacity that one-by-one calls waste; the same work completes for a fraction of the passes.
rules.how: Group independent requests within a stated latency window, use provider batch endpoints where latency tolerance allows, measure the per-item cost difference.

patterns.note: Inference call inside a loop; candidate for batching if items are independent.

verify.how: Per-item cost and latency measured batched vs sequential; latency budget respected.

limits: Interactive latency budgets can rule out batching; the measurement decides.

rules.title: Enforce the AI budget at runtime
rules.what: AI usage has runtime limits: max tokens in and out, max requests per user, timeouts, and cost tracking per feature.
rules.why: Without a runtime budget, one prompt loop or one runaway agent burns a day of compute in an hour, and nobody notices until the invoice. Budgets convert an anomaly into an alert.
rules.how: Per-feature token and request caps, streaming with an abort on runaway output, cost dashboards per feature, alert thresholds.

patterns.note: Very high or unlimited token budget; verify it is a deliberate choice.

verify.how: Runaway-request test: capped, alerted and logged within the budget.

rules.title: Count the whole cost of a successful task
rules.what: Measure the AI cost per completed user task, including retries, failed generations, tool calls and rework - not per API call.
rules.why: A cheap call rate can hide an expensive task: three retries, a failed tool loop and a regeneration make the 'successful' task cost five times the nominal call.
rules.how: Define the task unit, instrument the whole path (attempts, tool calls, human rework), report cost per completed task and its distribution.

verify.how: Cost-per-completed-task dashboard exists with attempts and rework counted.

limits: Human rework is observable imperfectly (edits, resubmissions); record the proxy used.

rules.title: Prefer RAG over fine-tuning for knowledge
rules.what: For injecting knowledge, prefer retrieval over fine-tuning unless measured evidence says otherwise; do not fine-tune to teach facts the model can retrieve.
rules.why: Fine-tuning pays its training cost up front and again at every model update, and it encodes knowledge that goes stale silently. Retrieval pays per use and updates with the source.
rules.how: Start with retrieval on curated sources; consider fine-tuning only for measured style/format gains that retrieval cannot reach; document the decision.

verify.how: Fine-tuning decisions record: what was tried with retrieval, the measured gap, the training cost.

limits: Some latency-critical tasks genuinely need baked-in knowledge; the evidence decides.

rules.title: Responsible AI is part of the scope
rules.what: AI work checks the responsible-AI basics: data permissions and provenance, model oversights, error handling for refusal/uncertainty, no silent personal data leakage to prompts.
rules.why: A service that is frugal but unfair or unlawful is not responsible; efficiency gains never buy back trust. Sobriety and responsibility are two floors of the same building.
rules.how: For any AI feature: name the data sources and their permissions, the human oversight path, and the failure behaviour. Load references/responsible-ai-charter.md when a charter assessment is requested.

verify.how: Feature documentation answers: sources/permissions, oversight, failure mode.

limits: Code cannot certify an organisation's compliance; the review lists evidence, not verdicts.

rules.title: Deterministic first, LLM for the ambiguous part
rules.what: Use a language model only for the genuinely ambiguous part of a task, and compare it against a non-LLM baseline (rules, regex, search, a small classifier) before adopting it.
rules.why: A model call costs orders of magnitude more compute than a deterministic function for the same answer on structured input, and adds latency, variance and failure modes.
rules.how: Write the baseline first; route only the cases the baseline cannot settle to the model; record quality and cost of both on the same evaluation set.

verify.how: Evaluation on a fixed set comparing the baseline and the model: quality, latency and cost per successful task.

rules.title: Measure AI consumption, do not estimate it
rules.what: Report the resources of an AI workload from measurement (tokens, GPU-hours, metered energy where available), with the method, the period and the uncertainty.
rules.why: Vendor ratios and per-token energy figures vary by orders of magnitude across models, hardware and load; an estimate quoted as a fact misleads every decision built on it.
rules.how: Log tokens in/out and calls per successful task; read GPU power from the platform (nvidia-smi, DCGM, cloud metrics); label any modelled value as a model.

verify.how: The figure cites its source (meter, log, model) and its uncertainty.

rules.title: Size self-hosted inference to the workload
rules.what: Before buying or reserving accelerators, quantise the model, try CPU for small models, move preprocessing to CPU, and justify GPU capacity with a utilisation measurement.
rules.why: An idle or oversized accelerator draws power and embodies manufacturing impact for work a smaller or quantised setup would handle.
rules.how: Try int8/int4 quantisation with an accuracy check; batch requests; monitor utilisation and temperature (DCGM) and right-size from the data.

verify.how: Utilisation and latency measured on the target workload; accuracy of the quantised model checked against the reference.

rules.title: Stream long outputs
rules.what: Stream long model outputs to the client and let users stop a generation they no longer need.
rules.why: Streaming shows useful text sooner and lets the user cancel early: tokens never generated are compute never spent.
rules.how: Use the streaming mode of the API; wire a stop control to request cancellation; cap max_tokens to the need.

patterns.note: Output cap absent or very large; check it matches the need.

verify.how: UI test: first tokens displayed before completion; stop control cancels the request server-side.

rules.title: Train and fine-tune on filtered data
rules.what: Deduplicate and filter training and fine-tuning datasets to what the task needs before spending compute on them.
rules.why: Duplicates and off-task data cost training compute and storage, and can degrade the model they were meant to improve.
rules.how: Deduplicate (exact and near-duplicate), filter by quality and relevance, document the dataset card with sizes before/after.

verify.how: Dataset card records filtering steps and sizes before/after.
